title: What must never enter a repository
objective: By the end of this lesson you can keep secrets, generated files, and local settings out of a repository permanently, and you know what to do when something sensitive gets committed anyway.

blocks.text: A repository should contain the source of the project — the things a person wrote — and nothing else. Three categories keep trying to sneak in: things that are generated, things that are personal to one machine, and things that are secret. The third one is the reason this lesson sits early in the course.
The ignore file: a list of what Git should not offer to track

blocks.caption: A .gitignore that covers the usual suspects
lines: # generated — rebuildable, so storing it wastes everyone's time
# an exception: keep this one even though the rule above would hide it

rows: Any file ending in .log, at any depth
A directory named build and everything inside it
Only at the repository root, not in subdirectories
PDFs directly inside docs, but not deeper
A directory named temp at any depth
An exception — track this even though *.log is ignored

blocks.title: Ignoring only applies to files Git is not already tracking
blocks.text: Adding a file to the ignore list does nothing if that file has already been committed — Git keeps tracking it. Stop tracking it with git rm --cached, then commit that removal. And note what this does not do: the file stays in every earlier commit.
Why generated files do not belong

items: They can be rebuilt from the source, so storing them adds nothing you cannot regenerate
They change on every build, so they fill the history with noise nobody reads
They cause conflicts constantly — two people build, two different outputs, one collision
They are enormous: a dependency folder commonly outweighs the entire source it belongs to

blocks.text: The one that actually hurts: committed credentials

An API key committed once is in the history permanently. If the repository is public, automated scanners find it within minutes — this is a well-known, continuously running class of attack, not a theoretical risk. If it is private, it is still readable by everyone with access, and by anyone who later gains access to any clone.

blocks.title: If a credential is committed, treat it as leaked
blocks.text: The first action is always to rotate it — revoke the key and issue a new one. Rewriting history is a separate, messier job that does not undo the exposure, because copies may already exist. Rotate first, then clean up. A key that has been rotated is worthless to whoever found it.

blocks.caption: Keeping credentials out by design
lines: # Commit an example, never the real thing:
cp .env .env.example        # then blank out every real value in the example
git add .env.example        # the real file stays ignored
# Check what you are about to commit — every time

blocks.title: The example-file convention
blocks.text: Commit an example file with the setting names present but the values blank or fake. New people copy it and fill in real values locally. The repository documents what configuration is needed without ever holding a real credential.

blocks.title: Prove the rules to yourself
steps: Run: mkdir -p node_modules && touch node_modules/x.js app.log
Run: git status              (neither appears — they are ignored)
Run: git add .gitignore && git commit -m "Ignore generated files"
Run: echo 'token=abc123' > local.conf && git add -f local.conf && git commit -m "Oops"
Run: echo 'local.conf' >> .gitignore && git status   (still tracked — ignoring came too late)
Run: git rm --cached local.conf && git commit -m "Stop tracking the local config"
Run: git log -p --all -- local.conf | head -20       (the value is still in history)
blocks.expected: Ignored files never appear, an already-tracked file keeps being tracked until you remove it from the index, and the last command shows the point of the whole lesson: the value is still readable in the earlier commit, which is why rotation — not deletion — is the fix.

cheatsheet: A repository holds source; keep out generated, personal, and secret files
The ignore file lists what Git should not offer to track
*.log any depth · build/ a directory · /file.txt root only · !keep.log an exception
Ignoring does not affect files that are already tracked
git rm --cached <file> stops tracking without deleting your copy
Removal does not erase the file from earlier commits
Committed credential = leaked credential: rotate first, clean up second
Commit an example file with blank values; keep the real one ignored
git ls-files | grep -Ei 'env|key|secret' audits what is already tracked

checkpoint.prompt: You add a file to the ignore list, but it keeps showing up in git status. Why?

choices.A: You need to commit the ignore file first for any rule to apply
choices.B: The ignore file only works after a restart
choices.C: The pattern must start with a slash

checkpoint.explanation: Ignore rules only apply to files Git is not tracking yet. Use git rm --cached to stop tracking it, then commit that. The ignore rule then keeps it out from that point forward.

checkpoint.prompt: An API key was committed and pushed an hour ago. What is the first thing to do?

choices.D: Delete the file and commit the deletion

checkpoint.explanation: Revoke it and issue a new one. Exposure has already happened and copies may exist. A rotated key is worthless to whoever has it; history cleanup is a separate follow-up job that does not undo the exposure.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is committing a build output directory a bad idea?

choices.D: It is rebuildable from source, changes on every build, causes constant conflicts, and is usually far larger than the project itself

checkpoint.explanation: Generated output adds size and noise while adding no information the source does not already contain.

checkpoint.prompt: What is the example-file convention for?

choices.A: An encrypted version of the configuration
choices.B: A committed file that documents which configuration values are needed, with blank or fake values
choices.C: A backup of the real configuration file
choices.D: A file Git reads automatically at build time

checkpoint.explanation: The real one never enters the repository. It gives newcomers the shape of the configuration without ever putting a working credential into the history.
